The Negative Binomial Family

Source: R/family.R
negative_binomial.Rd

Specifies a negative binomial response for glgpm() and specify_glgpm(), for counts that vary more than a Poisson model allows. A count \(y\) with exposure \(m\) given the random effects has mean \(\mu = m \exp(\eta)\), with the log link, and variance \(\mu + \mu^2 / \theta\), as in MASS::negative.binomial(theta). The size \(\theta\) is estimated unless fixed_pars = list(theta = ) of glgpm() holds it, and specify_glgpm() takes it as theta in its parameters. The negative binomial family is experimental and may change in a minor release.

Usage

negative_binomial(...)

# S3 method for class 'RiskMap_family'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

...

For negative_binomial(), not used, and a size given here stops, since it is held with fixed_pars instead. For print(), not used, and an error if given.

x

A family from negative_binomial(), whose print() method describes it and returns x invisibly.

Value

An object of class RiskMap_family.

Details

The exposure is given in the denominator of glgpm(), and is 1 for every count when it is not given. As \(\theta\) grows the model tends to the Poisson model with the same mean, and a fit whose size goes to that limit holds it there, as a variance estimated as zero is held, and says so in check_fit(). A fit that estimates the size reports it in coef(), print() and summary() as theta. Its start is the size of the negative binomial regression without the random effects, or start_pars$theta in glgpm(). With one observation per location, an estimated size can't be told apart from a nugget or from a random effect with one level per observation, so those are refused. A fit with an estimated size uses the sampled form of Monte Carlo maximum likelihood (see integrate_noise in set_control_mcml()), and its check for other maxima has no screen of short scales. MASS::negative.binomial(theta) is read as the negative binomial family with its size held at theta.

Given the size, the log-likelihood of a count is that of a binomial count of \(y\) successes in \(y + \theta\) trials with the logit link and the offset \(\log(m / \theta)\), plus terms in \(y\) and \(\theta\), which is how RiskMap fits it. The log-likelihood that a fit reports leaves out \(y \log m - \log y!\), as that of a Poisson fit does, so the two can be compared.

See also

glgpm(), stats::poisson()

Examples

negative_binomial()
#> The negative binomial family with the log link and its size estimated.
